beats.narration: Chapter 31 covers solid tumours organ by organ: 1,183 sentences, 159 of them mine to rule on. I worked through it over two days. 99 needed revision, 59 held up, and one I rejected outright, which came to 143 edits across 8 files. Chapter 32, on brain and spinal tumours, has 1,167 sentences. Of its 101, 58 needed revision, 40 held up, and 3 I left pending.

beats.new_visual_element: The right control number, the wrong treatment number
beats.narration: Two trials showed me how that happens. Chapter 32 quotes a trial of MRI during brain surgery as 81 percent complete removal against 68. The trial reported 96 against 68. Chapter 31 quotes a breast cancer trial as 27.6 months against 14.5. It was 24.8 against 14.5. In both, the comparison number is correct, and that is exactly why the wrong one slipped past review.

spendItems: The control number was right both times
props.costLine: The right half let the wrong half through.

beats.new_visual_element: A claim pointing the wrong way
beats.narration: Chapter 31 also has claims that point the wrong way. I counted eight. The clearest says smoking accounts for a larger share of lung cancer in women than in men. It is the reverse, about 95 percent in men and 90 in women, because more women with lung cancer have never smoked. A swap like that reads perfectly well, which is how it survives.

data.question: Where is smoking's share of lung cancer higher?

branches.label: MEN
branches.fix: More women with lung cancer never smoked.

resolver.label: THE CHAPTER SWAPPED THEM
resolver.detail: Never-smokers are 15.7 percent of women with lung cancer, 9.6 percent of men.

beats.new_visual_element: Approvals withdrawn since the chapter was written
beats.narration: Other claims were right once. The chapter lists five immunotherapies for advanced bladder cancer after chemotherapy, and two of them have since lost that approval. It also describes a late-line ovarian cancer treatment whose approvals were all withdrawn. That is the row I rejected, because the option the textbook describes no longer exists.

beats.new_visual_element: When the audit itself was wrong
beats.narration: Chapter 32 also made me check the audit itself. One finding gave a hazard ratio for a trial and cited a paper. When I opened the paper, it was a different trial: 66 patients, in Tel Aviv. Another flagged a quotation the chapter had right. And three figures I could not confirm, because the abstract did not have them and I could not get the full text. I left those pending rather than guess.

beats.narration: What I keep from these two is a habit. When a comparison has a number I recognise, I check the other number first. When a drug is described as approved, I check whether it still is. And when I cannot confirm something, I say so in the record instead of filling the gap.
